object_types.name: Incident
object_types.definition: An incident that is tracked through triage, declaration, mitigation, resolution, and closure. Never deleted once created.

source_references.excerpt: Incident number. INC-, then a sequence.
Unique. And we never delete incidents, which becomes relevant later.

object_types.name: IncidentNumber
object_types.definition: The unique identifier of an incident, formatted as INC- followed by a sequence.

source_references.excerpt: Incident number. INC-, then a sequence.

object_types.name: Alert
object_types.definition: A signal from the monitoring platform (automatic or manually raised) indicating a possible issue.

source_references.excerpt: And an alert -- identified how? Alert ID. Comes from the monitoring platform.
It's a manual alert but it's still an alert.

object_types.name: AlertId
object_types.definition: The identifier of an alert, issued by the monitoring platform.

source_references.excerpt: Alert ID. Comes from the monitoring platform.

object_types.name: Ticket
object_types.definition: A customer support ticket, possibly reporting an incident.

object_types.name: Service
object_types.definition: A service in the service catalogue, owned by a team, that can be affected by incidents.

object_types.name: ServiceName
object_types.definition: The unique name of a service.

source_references.excerpt: Service name. They're unique, we enforce it in the catalogue.

object_types.name: Team
object_types.definition: A team that owns one or more services.

A team. Services are owned by teams. People move.

object_types.name: Person
object_types.definition: An individual who can act as incident commander for the duration of an incident.

source_references.excerpt: The incident commander. One person, named, and it's a role for the duration, not a job title.

object_types.name: Severity

object_types.name: Priority
object_types.definition: The priority level of an incident describing customer urgency.

Priority is about customer urgency.

object_types.name: IncidentState
object_types.definition: The current state of an incident.

inferred_constraints.fact_type: Incident is a duplicate of Incident
inferred_constraints.description: Duplicate chains should not form cycles and, per intent, should point directly at a primary rather than chaining (rule stated as intended but not enforced today).

source_references.excerpt: Can a chain form? B duplicates A, C duplicates B? It shouldn't. The intent is that everything points at the primary directly. ... It's wrong. If C duplicates B and B duplicates A, then C should point at A.
That's the rule as intended. It's not enforced.

ambiguities.description: The duplicate-chain rule (duplicates should point directly at a primary, no chains, primary is not itself a duplicate) is stated as the intended rule but is explicitly not enforced in the system today. Should the model enforce acyclicity/depth-1 strictly, or reflect the current unenforced reality?

source_references.excerpt: nothing stops you making a chain and I've seen two-deep ones. ... That's the rule as intended. It's not enforced.

source_references.excerpt: The model today captures the five states and does not include any concept of a cause classification, because there isn't one to capture.
That's a decision about what we report to the board, and Ravi owns that. ... I'll raise it with Ravi.

ambiguities.description: "Owner" is an overloaded term: it can mean the Incident Commander (a per-incident role held by a person) or the Service Owner (a standing team assignment unrelated to any particular incident). The transcript flags this as a recurring source of confusion in practice.

source_references.excerpt: Nadia, you said commander is a role, not a job title. Is there a different sense of owner? ... And in a channel, "who owns this?" means either. It's genuinely ambiguous every single time.

ambiguities.description: "Severity" vs "Priority" are frequently conflated colloquially (people say "sev" to mean either), even though the model treats them as independent mandatory single-valued attributes. This is a terminology/communication ambiguity rather than a modeling gap, but worth flagging since it caused real incidents of miscommunication.

source_references.excerpt: Which is completely different, and this is the single biggest source of miscommunication in the company. ... And people say "sev" when they mean either.

ambiguities.description: Severity and priority changes over time are tracked only in a separate 'timeline' of events, not modeled here; the Incident record only carries the current value. Should the timeline/history of severity and priority changes be modeled as a formal fact type (temporal/historical tracking) rather than only current-state attributes?

source_references.excerpt: Severity gets revised as we understand the blast radius. ... In the timeline, as events. The incident record carries the current severity.

ambiguities.description: The 'monitoring' status Owen mentions is explicitly excluded from the model because it is not a formal state in the system dropdown, despite being informally used. Confirm this exclusion is correct and no additional informal states exist elsewhere.

source_references.excerpt: There's also "monitoring," which sits between mitigated and resolved. ... If it's not in the system I'm not modelling it. Five states.
